record.original_question: For semigroup elements a and b, define a ∼p b when there exist u and v in the semigroup with a = uv and b = vu. If a semigroup has the property that ∼p is transitive in every variant of that semigroup, where the variant at an element c has multiplication x ◦ y = xcy, must ∼p already be transitive in the original semigroup?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.22 from [3] asks whether ∼p must be transitive for a semigroup if it is transitive for all of the semigroup’s variants.

This example is generated by {5, 6, 7} with the following properties: (1) 5 · 6 = 5 · 7, (2) 6 · 5 6∼p 7 · 5, and (3) any word of length at least 3 equals 0. (1) and (2) imply ∼p is not transitive for S, but (3) implies ∼p is transitive for every variant.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a semigroup. For $a,b\in S$, write $a\sim_p b$ (the primary equivalence) if there exist $u,v\in S$ such that $a=uv$ and $b=vu$. For each $c\in S$, the variant of $S$ at $c$ is the semigroup $S^c$ with underlying set $S$ and multiplication $x\circ_c y := xcy$; the relation $\sim_p$ is defined analogously inside each variant $S^c$.

Question: Does there exist a semigroup $S$ such that the relation $\sim_p$ is transitive in every variant $S^c$ ($c\in S$), yet $\sim_p$ is not transitive in $S$ itself? Equivalently, must transitivity of $\sim_p$ in every variant of $S$ force transitivity of $\sim_p$ in $S$?

status_evidence.title: Counterexample construction
status_evidence.snippet: An example generated by {5,6,7} with 5·6 = 5·7, 6·5 ≁p 7·5, and every word of length ≥ 3 equal to 0; properties imply ∼p is not transitive for S, but ∼p is transitive for every variant.
status_evidence.claim: A semigroup is exhibited in which ∼p is transitive in every variant but not in the semigroup itself, answering the question in the negative.
